source.title: Variation Structures: Results and Open Problems

accepted.question_text: For an invariant i of isolated hypersurface germs f:(C^{n+2},0)->(C,0) that can be written as f=p∘ϕ with ϕ:(C^{n+2},0)->(C^2,0) an isolated complete intersection singularity and p:(C^2,0)->(C,0) a curve singularity, what category C(i) of supplementary coefficient structures on (C^2,0) or on the local complement of the discriminant germ Δ⊂(C^2,0) should be used so that ϕ determines an element S(ϕ)∈C(i) and i(f) can be computed from p and S(ϕ)? In particular, can one define a generalized Dynkin diagram D(p,S), for an isolated curve singularity p and S∈C(i), such that D(p,S(ϕ)) is the Dynkin diagram of f=p∘ϕ whenever f has an isolated singularity?

evidence.quote: Studying the invariants of isolated hypersurface germs f : (Cn+2 , 0) → (C, 0), it is very useful to consider composed germs f = p ◦ ϕ, where ϕ : (Cn+2 , 0) → (C2 , 0) has a manageable discriminant space (for example: ϕ is an isolated complete intersection singularity, in short ICIS), and p : (C2 , 0) → (C, 0) is a curve singularity.

Problem # 1. Find the category C(i) for other invariants. For example, ﬁnd a category C(i) such that any ICIS ϕ (as above) gives an element S(ϕ) ∈ C(i). Moreover, deﬁne a “generalized Dynkin diagram” D(p, S) for any (isolated) curve singularity p and S ∈ C(i) in such a way that D(p, S(ϕ)) is the Dynkin diagram of f = p ◦ ϕ (provided that f has isolated singularity).

accepted.question_text: Given two ε-hermitian variation structures, where such a structure for a group G is a quadruple (U;b,ρ,V) consisting of an ε-hermitian form b, a representation ρ:G->Aut(U;b), and a twisted homomorphism V:G->Hom(U*,U) satisfying θ^{-1}∘V(g)*=-εV(g)∘ρ(g)* and V(g)∘b=ρ(g)-I, how should their tensor product be defined in full generality? The answer should specify the resulting vector space, hermitian form, group representation, variation map, and sign convention, extending the known simple case in which the automorphism of the tensor product satisfies ⊗h=-εε1ε2 h1⊗h2.

evidence.quote: Definition. An ϵ–hermitian variation structure of the group G is a system V = (U ; b, ρ, V ) such that b is an ϵ–hermitian (maybe degenerate) form, ρ is a representation of G in Aut(U ; b), V is a twisted–homeomorphism, and they satify the following compatibility conditions for any g ∈ G: (i) θ−1 ◦ V (g)∗ = −ϵV (g) ◦ ρ(g)∗ , and (ii) V (g) ◦ b = ρ(g) − I.

If Vi , (i = 1, 2) are simple ϵi –hermitian variation structures, then the tensor product V1 ⊗ V2 deﬁnes a new simple ϵ–structure (for any ϵ). The corresponding automorphisms are related by ⊗ h = −ϵϵ1 ϵ2 h1 ⊗ h2 .
Problem # 2. Find the tensor product of two variation structures.

accepted.question_text: Classify all ε-hermitian variation structures for G=Z, writing a structure as (U;b,h,V) with h=ρ(1) and V=V(1), beyond the already classified simple structures. The classification should include degenerate and non-simple cases such as indecomposable variation structures whose monodromy h has more than one Jordan block, identify natural restrictions that occur for simple structures V(f) coming from isolated hypersurface singularities, and classify the structures satisfying those restrictions, including a class containing the structures produced by hypersurface singularities with one-dimensional singular locus.

evidence.quote: They deﬁne an indecomposable (+1)-HVS, but the automorphism h has two Jordan blocks. Note that even the associated (degenerate) isometric structure (b, h) is indecomposable.
In this section G = Z and the system V = (U ; b, h, V ) denotes h = ρ(1) and V = V (1).

Problem # 3. Classify the variation structures for G = Z (cf. Example 11). Any hypersurface isolated singularity gives a simple variation structure (of G = Z) (cf. Example 4). Find natural restrictions provided by the singularity theory, and classify variation structures with the corresponding restrictions. Classify a class of variation structures which includes the structures given by hypersurface singularities with one–dimensional singular locus.

accepted.question_text: Let ϕ be an isolated complete intersection singularity with two-dimensional base space and discriminant locus Δ. For an embedded resolution (U,E)->(B,Δ), let Δ0 be an irreducible component of Δ, let its strict transform be Δ~0, set P=Δ~0∩E, and let UP be a small neighbourhood of P in U. The restriction of the variation structure V(ϕ) to Z^2=π1(UP minus E) gives a variation structure of G=Z^2. What natural restrictions on Z^2-variation structures are forced by this local geometric situation, and how can the Z^2-variation structures satisfying those restrictions be classified?
accepted.context_brief: Geometric Z^2 restrictions near a discriminant component

evidence.quote: ϕ : (Cn+2 , 0) → (C2 , 0) has a manageable discriminant space (for example: ϕ is an isolated complete intersection singularity, in short ICIS)

Problem # 4. Let ϕ be an ICIS with two–dimensional base space (as in the introduction). Let (U, E) → (B, ∆) be an embedded resolution of its discriminant locus. Let ∆0 be one of the irreducible components of ∆, ∆˜0 its strict transform, and ﬁnally P = ∆˜0 ∩ E. Let UP be a small neighbourhood of the point P in U . The variation structure V(ϕ) restricted to the subgroup Z2 = π1 (UP \E) gives a variation structure of the group G = Z2 . Now, ﬁnd a natural restriction which is provided by this geometric situation and classify variation structures of the group G with this restriction.

accepted.question_text: For an isolated complete intersection singularity ϕ with two-dimensional base space and the embedded-resolution local setup that restricts V(ϕ) to a Z^2-variation structure near a point P on the exceptional divisor, a natural limit mixed Hodge structure carries a Z^2 action via the semisimple part of the monodromy representation. Can the isolated-hypersurface theorem connecting the topological invariant V(f) with the Hodge-theoretical primitive invariants pλ^{a,b}(f), and in particular showing that Hodge numbers determine the real Seifert form, be extended to this Z^2 limit mixed-Hodge setting?

evidence.quote: The connection between the topological invariant V(f ) and the Hodge theoretical invariants pλa,b (f ) is given in the following Theorem.[11]
In particular, the Hodge numbers determine the real Seifert form.

Problem # 5. In the context of Problem # 4 there is a natural limit mixed Hodge structure with the action of Z2 (via the semi–simple part of the monodromy representation) ([19], see also [15] and [17]). Extend the above Theorem to this case.

accepted.question_text: Fix n. Which simple ε-hermitian variation structures for G=Z occur as V(f) for some isolated hypersurface singularity f:(C^{n+1},0)->(C,0), where V(f) is generated by the middle homology of the Milnor fiber, intersection form, monodromy, and variation map? Give a complete characterization, taking into account known necessary restrictions such as the absence of components Wλ^{n+1-s}((-1)^{n+1}) and the condition that a Jordan block of monodromy size n+1 for eigenvalue not equal to 1 forces a Jordan block of size n for eigenvalue 1.

evidence.quote: An important element in HVϵs (Z), provided by an isolated hypersurface singularity f , is V(f ) generated by (U ; b, ρ(1), V (1)) = (middle homology of the Milnor ﬁber of f ; intersection form, monodromy, variation map).
Proposition.[11] The structures Wλn+1−s ((−1)n+1 ) do not appear in the decomposition of V(f ) for any isolated singularity f : (Cn+1 , 0) → (C, 0).

Proposition. If f : (Cn+1 , 0) → (C, 0) is an isolated singularity such that its monodromy h has a Jordan block of size n + 1 (necessarily for an eigenvalue ̸= 1), then h has a Jordan block of size n for the eigenvalue = 1.
Problem # 6. For a ﬁxed n, ﬁnd the complete set of simple variation structures (G = Z) which are given by isolated hypersurface singularities.

accepted.question_text: For ε-hermitian variation structures of a group G, form the Witt group WVε(G) by quotienting isomorphism classes under direct sum by hyperbolic structures. For G=Z^k, the known classification decomposes WVε(G) over unitary characters χ and has summand Z for χ≠1 and Z2 for χ=1. How can this Witt-group classification be extended to more general groups, ideally to local fundamental groups of complements of curve singularities p^{-1}(0)⊂(C^2,0)?

evidence.quote: In particular, the semigroup W Vϵ (G) = (HVϵ (G)/{hyperbolic structures}, ⊕) is actually a group. It is called the Witt group of the variation structures of G.
W Vϵ (Zk )χ = { Z if χ ∈ Ĝ − {1} Z2 if χ = 1. The generators are (C; ±i(1−ϵ)/2 , χ, ±(χ − 1)i(ϵ−1)/2 ) if χ ̸= 1, and (C; 0, 1, 0) if χ = 1.

Problem # 7. Extend the above classiﬁcation for more general groups. (It would be ideal to have a classiﬁcation theorem for the local fundamental groups of complements of curve singularities p−1 (0) ⊂ (C2 , 0).)

accepted.question_text: Given an ε-hermitian variation structure V=(U;b,ρ,V) of a group G, Wall's triple-kernel signature defines a homogeneous 2-cocycle σ(V;·,·,·) and hence a semigroup morphism c1:HVε(G)->H^2(G,Z). What are the higher-dimensional analogues of this class c1 in H^{2q}(G,Z)?

evidence.quote: Therefore σ(V; K1 , K2 , K3 ) deﬁnes a homogeneous cocycle of the group G in Z (Z is considered with the trivial G–action).
The semigroup morphism c1 : HVϵ (G) → H 2 (G, Z), c1 (V) = σ(V; ·, ·, ·) is not trivial in general.
Problem # 8. Find the higher dimensional analogues of c1 in H 2q (G, Z).

accepted.question_text: Let ηV(g) be the eta-invariant of an ε-hermitian variation structure V evaluated at g∈G, and let σ(V;Ke,Kg,Kh) be Wall's cocycle built from the kernels Kg={(φ,u):V(g)φ=u}. For which variation structures V, or for which groups G, does the eta-invariant satisfy the coboundary identity δ(η)=-σ, i.e. σ(V;Ke,Kg,Kh)=-η(g)-η(g^{-1}h)+η(h), as is known when G is finitely generated abelian?

evidence.quote: The eta–invariant ηV (g) is deﬁned by the sum χ ηV (g)χ
Theorem. If G is a (ﬁnitely generated) abelian group then: σ(V; Ke , Kg , Kh ) = −η(g) − η(g −1 h) + η(h). In particular δ(η) = −σ.
Problem # 9. Characterize variation structures V (or groups G) with the property δ(η) = −σ.

accepted.question_text: Consider composed germs f=p∘ϕ, where ϕ:(C^{n+2},0)->(C^2,0) has discriminant Δ and p:(C^2,0)->(C,0) is a reduced irreducible curve singularity. The signature σ(f) can be expressed through contributions from the splice diagram of p^{-1}(0)∪Δ, and abelian variation-structure data over a Seifert component can be computed from eta-invariants of V(ϕ). Which composed germs f=p∘ϕ have the stronger property that σ(f) can be computed only from the eta-invariant η_{V(ϕ)} and the curve singularity p?

evidence.quote: Our goal is to compute σ(f ). For simplicity, assume that p is reduced and irreducible. Consider the splice diagram Γ(p, ∆) of the multilink determined by p−1 (0)∪ ∆ ⊂ (C2 , 0), where the multiplicity of p−1 (0) is 1, and the other multiplicities are zero.
Theorem.[13] The signature σ(f ) is a sum σ(f ) = nodes σ(Σ, ρ) over the nodes of Γ(p, ∆)
(b) If the variation structure above Σ is abelian, then: σ(Σ, ρ) = ∑r 1=1 ni · η(Li mi/ni Mi m′i/ni ).
Problem # 10. Characterize composed germs f = p ◦ ϕ such that σ(f ) can be computed only in terms of ηV(ϕ) and p.

accepted.question_text: For an isolated complete intersection singularity ϕ with two-dimensional base and an embedded-resolution local model (U,E)->(B,Δ), the restriction of V(ϕ) near P=Δ~0∩E gives a Z^2-variation structure. Compute the eta-invariant of this Z^2-variation structure in terms of the natural limit mixed Hodge structure with Z^2 action via the semisimple monodromy representation.
